Every single day on average, it moves 7 basis points. For the last 20 years, it moved 3.4 on average. You got a lot of moving around.

Over the last 20 years it was 4.4. Once again, not quite double, but, you know, certainly near that. You know, that was the mountain that we were fighting, the uphill battle against. I think they've done a very, very good job about that. I hope that addresses your question.
Matthew Howlett
Senior Research Analyst, B. Riley Securities
Yeah, it does. Thank you. I guess last question on just, you know, on topic of just capital. I mean, the stock's, you know, held up. I mean, it's above book here. You look at, you know, the preferred markets. You know, I know you don't have a crystal ball, but what do you think all the preferreds for the mortgage REITs are trading below?
It's sort of, to me, you know, as you outlined on your statement, it's one of the best environments you've seen in a while. Any sense on, you know, when the preferred market would open up and would you access that? It looks like your capital, you have room to add some preferred in the capital structure.
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
We spend every quarter on this very subject. Let's take a look at it right now. When the 10-year note was trading at, you know, 1.25% to 2%, it would make sense that six and a half, seven, 7.25 coupon preferred would be trading at or around their $25 par. 10-year worked
Matthew Howlett
Senior Research Analyst, B. Riley Securities
Right
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Its way up to 275 to 350, you could see that just nominally that return is not enough to compete with risk-free treasuries. In our opinion, the preferreds are trading more or less where they make sense. Now, there's two ways to look at what you could do with your preferreds at this point in time. You could buy some back at $21 a share. I believe the float for all of our peers in whether it's a 6.5 or 7.5 coupon, they all seem to be trading $20 to 21.50. It's not as accretive to book value as you would think. Now, the real yields on those are like 8.25 to 8.75 because they're trading under par.
Mark and his team can invest at 12, 14, 16, maybe even 18% right now. We have better investment opportunities in our primary asset class of agency mortgages rather than buying back the preferreds. What you commented on was that you thought we had a good balance between preferreds currently and the amount of common equity that we have outstanding. We agree with that 100%. Preferreds start trading above par again. If our common equity is larger, we might look at issuing those, but that's not something that we're interested in doing right now for all the reasons I just mentioned.
Matthew Howlett
Senior Research Analyst, B. Riley Securities
Right. Well, you have 7%, I think, on the current preferred. I mean, with the returns available today, would you issue at 7.5%, 8% if that was to tighten a little bit and open up? Would it make sense? It looks like it would be accretive where you mentioned returns are a great agency.
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
I think it's unlikely at this point we'd be issuing any coupons above where our current outstanding issue is. Once again, if we traded up toward par again, and we felt we wanted to access the capital markets in that fashion, we'd probably increase the size of that issue. We'll remind you twice in our history we've bought issues out. We bought all the As back. We bought all the B issues.
Matthew Howlett
Senior Research Analyst, B. Riley Securities
Yep.
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
A large issue, too. Bought all the Bs back. We'll see what the future, you know, presents itself. We're actively use that class of, you know, equity structure actively as part of the way we run our company. Yes, I really appreciate the question because not enough people understand the value in having that optionality.
Matthew Howlett
Senior Research Analyst, B. Riley Securities
Yeah, it just looks like they're at incredible discounts today. Yeah, thanks, Scott. That really helps. Thanks, Jeff.
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Thank you.

Once again, if you would like to ask a question, please press star and then one. Our next question comes from Christopher Nolan from Ladenburg Thalmann. Please go ahead with your question.

Hey, Jeff. Most of my questions have been asked. Just a clarification on your earlier comments in terms of the earnings run rate, given the shift into the higher yielding agencies. Should we be expecting the management fee waiver to decline in H2?

Andrew, do we have questions?

Got it. Just on the dividend comment. You know, if I take the current dividend divided by your updated April book value, you know, that gives me, you know, kind of a number north of, you know, a 15% required return to kind of generate that, and that would be kind of after expenses. You know, you're talking 12% to 15% returns that you're seeing in the market. You know, just curious as to kind of your commentary around the comfort in that dividend level.
Jeffrey Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Based on the historic assets that we own and based on the current investment opportunities, we definitely can support that dividend. We have not had a longer-term discussion with the board in terms of Q3 or Q4 yet, but we currently feel very comfortable with what we're paying, and that supports Scott's comments.
Douglas Harter
Director, Credit Suisse
Okay. Thank you.
Jeffrey Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Thank you very much.
Operator
The next question comes from Trevor Cranston with JMP Securities. Please go ahead.
Trevor Cranston
Managing Director, JMP Securities
Hey, thanks. You know, there's obviously a lot of volatility and spread widening in Q1. Can you guys talk about kind of where you see things today? You know, how much risk you see of additional widening in the MBS market? You know, what your thoughts are on the potential for continued great volatility and Fed policy going forward over the rest of the year. Thanks.
Jeffrey Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
You wouldn't have thought, looking at 15 February 2020, that we'd be looking at investment opportunities 26 months later in the 12% to 15% area, because that's about 500 basis points better than what we were looking at then. I think that those changes highlight the risks that are inherent in the current environment. The geopolitical risks we can't do anything about. They're there. We respect them. We're being cautious about them, and we understand that they could be existential. We just don't know how crazy they could get. However, in the mortgage spread widening, we look back through the subprime crisis, which I think highlights how bad things can get. We're within a standard deviation or so of being normal on that. We are not fully invested, but we are adequately invested.
As Scott said in his comments and as we've said in our monthly company updates, we took more than $2 billion of treasuries and reinvested them into mortgages, but we did it over a 10- or 12-week period, and we caught some of the widest spreads. You know, we've also bought some assets a little tighter than we wanted to. We've left some cash on the table to reinvest if we do get a widening. As I said, we are very respectful of the risks that are out there, and we're cautiously, you know, watching those. We're probably not investing that last of opportunities of cash that we have as I said, are being respectful of that.
In terms of the second question that you asked, I don't think that the capital markets can let mortgage spreads get crazy wide for a long period of time. If they get to levered returns of 18% to 20%, it would probably be very short-lived. Even the high-yield indices have not, you know, we've gone out like what? 110 basis points or so. You know. You know. Anyway, that's our thoughts on that. I hope that answers your question.
Trevor Cranston
Managing Director, JMP Securities
Yeah, that's helpful. In terms of the coupon positioning of the portfolio, you guys have obviously been moving up in coupon somewhat. Can you maybe just talk about kind of what the pace you'd expect that rotation to continue at? You know, if you're or if you're comfortable continuing to own the larger discount bonds that you guys currently have in the portfolio.
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Hey, Trevor, this is Mark. I believe we're probably almost done with kind of rotating out of some of the lower coupons and the upper coupons. Mainly that's because, you know, the lower coupons have pretty much fully extended. They have good convexities, and they're good assets. When you look at our portfolio at our next update, you'll probably see us maintain most of those lower coupons. Most all the reinvestments are gonna go in the upper coupons. We've done, for the most part, all the rotation out. There'll be some little things on the end, but we really like the assets in the lower coupon just because they've extended so much already and the convexities are great.
Trevor Cranston
Managing Director, JMP Securities
Sure. Okay. That's helpful. Thank you.
Operator
The next question comes from Christopher Nolan with Ladenburg Thalmann. Please go ahead.
Christopher Nolan
SVP, Ladenburg Thalmann
Hey, guys. Just a question for Jim. Net interest income in the quarter sort of seemed to go up a bit quarter-over-quarter. Just trying to get a clarification why?
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Well, that's Mark. Net interest income between Q4 and Q1, is that what you're asking?
Christopher Nolan
SVP, Ladenburg Thalmann
Yeah.
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
It's just gonna be some rotation into some different bonds, but also amortization expense has slowed.
Christopher Nolan
SVP, Ladenburg Thalmann
Great. I was checking out the Q, and I just saw that your haircuts on your repo funding has actually gone down this quarter, which I found surprising given all the turbulence going on in the MBS market. Was that related to Buckler or is there any color you can provide on that?
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
No. That is, you know, the clearing market in repo on haircuts has declined, as I think more and more the counterparties are getting comfortable with what's the risk in holding MBS, agency MBS. We've actually got our counterparties to lower haircuts.
James Mountain
CFO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Yeah. That was a result of some actual outreach and conversation, trying to make sure everybody was, you know, meeting the market leader, and we're sort of most favored nation positions with all of our counterparties.
Jeffrey Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
You know, Christopher, I would note that in the Treasury market, many of the dealers have no haircuts at all. If you go back to the subprime crisis, and it's interesting, haircuts went from 3% to 4% up to 6% to 7%, 8% for 3 to 6 months, and we haven't seen that right now. We would suggest that the banks are characterizing the current environment as not being as risky as that and those haircuts and the, you know, despite the widening that's happened in mortgages, the, you know, volatility they're very comfortable with. I think that actually makes us somewhat comfortable with our increased investment in MBS.
Christopher Nolan
SVP, Ladenburg Thalmann
Okay. It sounds like there's a disconnect between how the banks are viewing the MBS market and what the credit spreads are saying.
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Well, I think they've gotten more comfortable with the fact that over time, you know, how often have mortgages dropped, you know, three or four points in a day? Because remember, they have our collateral, so they can sell it any time. It's bankruptcy remote. I think they're just more comfortable that they're not gonna see it, you know, greater than three-point drop in a day on the collateral we own. It's very liquid.
James Mountain
CFO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Well, perhaps a little bit too that, as repo rates are going up from, you know, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 basis points to 50 basis points. You know, we've seen new entrants in the market, and so the attractiveness of repo as an asset to them seems to be increasing and haircuts just, you know, one of the terms upon which they can compete for balances.
Christopher Nolan
SVP, Ladenburg Thalmann
Got it. Okay, thanks, guys.
Jeffrey Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Thank you.
Operator
Again, if you have a question, please press star then one. The next question comes from Matthew Howlett with Nomura. Please go ahead.
Matthew Howlett
Analyst, Nomura
Oh, oh, hey guys. Just a question on historical context, where MBS spreads are, you know, on a nominal or an OAS basis. Just like to hear where they are today versus, you know, different points in time, taper tantrum, financial crisis.
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
I'm going to have to pull up a chart here. But, you know, we think when we look at our analytics, you know, on a Z-spread basis, Fannie fours are about 110. OAS is obviously gonna be lower than that just because of the way the metric works. TBA spreads are probably in the, you know, in the mid-50s. We would say that TBA is tighter than agency MBS. It's definitely wider. On a Treasury OAS basis, one of the charts we look at is Treasury OAS on a historical basis. In general, the coupon stack is on the average of where the Fed has been buying, but it's below the long-term average of when they're not buying.
That's why we do think there's still some widening when the Fed decides to really stop and maybe actually sell, you know, 10 or 15 basis points. In general, mortgages are much, much wider than they were, you know, just a few months ago. That's why Jeff said earlier, you know, they're attractive and we've been, you know, slowly buying some over time.
Jeffrey Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
We run a number of different charts, and the charts have break-evens to when the Fed is buying to when they're not buying, and then we look at the crises thing. There was a period about eight or 12 business days ago where we were actually OAS spreads were well north of that. Mortgages actually performed well net of one day over the last week. We're just inside the net average of non-Fed buying over the last 12 years. Now, hopefully that's helpful to you. One of our largest counterparties actually puts out a chart of current coupons, and we follow that chart, and I think that's the best way to look at it.
Matthew Howlett
Analyst, Nomura
I think about the current environment, if they stay at these levels or they go wider, that's gonna be good for you know spread and you know core ROE, and if they tighten, I mean, you'll pick that up in book value. I mean, how do I think about you know sort of the risk return trade-off if we just stay at this current environment or they widen? That's good for reinvestment and then good for shareholders or if things do tighten, we'll see the big rebound in book.
Jeffrey Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
If things tighten, generally you would expect book value to go up. It doesn't always work that way because of the other events, but we would expect that to be the case. We think the vast majority of widening has taken place here, okay? Everybody knows the Fed's out, and everybody expects the Fed to go ahead and sell some assets, and I believe that that's priced into mortgage OAS right now. As I said earlier in my comments, we're extremely respectful of the fact that they could widen a little bit more, and we are ready if and when that happens to reinvest. That being said, when they do widen, book value generally has a proclivity to go down a bit. They tighten, book value generally has a proclivity to go up.
The investment opportunities now and if things widen are better. That is correct.
Matthew Howlett
Analyst, Nomura
Great. Then last question, I mean it looks like you got the liability side. You're pretty much termed out with I think you said 116% and you're good all the way up to the 275 through, you know, through the derivatives. Is there you mentioned long-dated, you know, repo maybe. But just is there anything else you're looking to do on, you know, the liability side of the balance sheet as you enter the, you know, what could be a rate hiking cycle? Or do you feel like you've pretty much done everything and, you know, and you're sort of well-positioned for it?
Jeffrey Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
As Scott said in his comments and as well as our press release said, we have more than 100% of our repo balances swapped out right now. What that means is as repo rates go up, we pay fixed on our swaps and our fixed rate is locked in, generally at lower rates than the market is right now. Then the receiver side would generally go up as well with repo rates. Those definitely offset each other. We look at that as very comforting in terms of our liability balance. As we increase our assets, and as we said also at this point, we're not generally increasing our leverage until we see some great opportunities. We would put more swaps on the book to offset that risk.
Matthew Howlett
Analyst, Nomura
Great. Thanks, Jeff.
Jeffrey Zimmer
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Thank you. Good to hear from you. Hadn't been a while.
Operator
This concludes our question and answer session. I would like to turn the conference back over to James Mountain for any closing remarks.
James Mountain
CFO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Let me end where we began, thanking you all for joining us this morning and for your interest in ARMOUR Residential REIT. We're always interested in conversations with shareholders and analysts. If anything comes up between now and the next time we're together in this forum, don't hesitate to reach out.

content.text:
Operator
Good morning, and welcome to the ARMOUR Residential REIT's Q4 and Full Year 2021 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. Should you need assistance, please signal a conference specialist by pressing star, then zero on your telephone keypad. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star, then one on your telephone keypad. To withdraw your question, please press star, then two. Please note this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Jim Mountain, Chief Financial Officer. Please go ahead.
Jim Mountain
CFO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Thank you, Andrew, and thank you all for joining our call this morning to discuss ARMOUR's Q4 2021 results. I'm joined today by ARMOUR's Co-CEO, Scott Ulm and Jeff Zimmer, and Mark Gruber, our Chief Investment Officer. By now, everyone has access to ARMOUR's earnings release, which can be found on ARMOUR's website, www.armourreit.com. This conference call may contain statements that are not recitations of historical fact and therefore constitute forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. All such forward-looking statements are intended to be subject to the safe harbor provisions provided by the Reform Act.
Actual outcomes and results could differ materially from the outcomes and results expressed or implied by the forward-looking statements due to the impact of many factors beyond the control of ARMOUR. Certain factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those contained in the forward-looking statements are included in the Risk Factors section of ARMOUR's periodic reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Copies are available on the SEC's website at www.sec.gov. All forward-looking statements included in this conference call are made only as of today's date and are subject to change without notice. We disclaim any obligation to update our forward-looking statements unless required by law. Also, our discussion today may include references to certain non-GAAP measures. A reconciliation of these measures to the most comparable GAAP measure is included in our earnings release.
An online replay of this conference call will be available on ARMOUR's website shortly and will continue for one year. Since we last spoke, interest rates in mortgage markets have been marked by choppy waters. ARMOUR's quarter-end book value was $10.33 per common share, down $0.76 from 30 September 2021. This quarter-over-quarter decrease reflects spread widening across our MBS portfolio, which is likely the result of the market ruminating on talk of inflation, Fed interest rate hikes, and future reductions in agency mortgage purchases. We expect this tightening and tapering market will be with us for a while, and we're optimistic that it will remain relatively orderly and avoid throwing another tantrum. For an apples-to-apples comparison across the sector, book value was $9.76 per common share on 31 January 2022.
As the close of business on 15 February 2022, we estimated ARMOUR's book value per common share to be approximately $9.17. While spread widening negatively impacts the current market value of our existing MBS portfolio, it also reflects increasing current asset yields and improving opportunities for new MBS investments. At 31 December 2021, ARMOUR's portfolio consisted of $4.4 billion of agency securities and TBA positions, representing another $4.5 billion. We also had $200 million of US Treasury securities. Since then, ARMOUR has reduced its agency and TBA portfolio by $2.9 billion and increased its US Treasury position by $1.6 billion to be ready to take advantage of those improving opportunities. ARMOUR's Q4 comprehensive loss was $37.8 million, which includes $20.8 million of GAAP net loss.
Attributable earnings, which exclude gains or losses from securities sales and early termination of derivatives, as well as market value adjustments, but it does include TBA drop income, was $27.7 million or $0.27 per common share. During Q4, ARMOUR issued 6,386,724 shares of common stock through the ATM programs, raising $67.5 million of capital after fees and expenses. As we've discussed on prior calls, increases in our common share base reduce per share administrative costs. For the full year, ARMOUR's common share count is up 44%, which reduces the administrative expense load by $0.17 per common share on an annualized pro forma basis. ARMOUR Capital Management, the company's external manager, continues to waive a portion of its management fee.
The waiver currently offsets $650,000 of operating expenses each month. The company paid dividends of $0.10 per common share for each month in Q4, for a total of $30.9 million. ARMOUR maintained that monthly dividend rate of $0.10 per share with the recently announced March 2022 common dividend. The Series C preferred stock dividends for Q1 2022 have also been declared at the contractual rate of 7% per annum. Now I'll turn the call over to Co-Chief Executive Officer Scott Ulm to discuss ARMOUR's portfolio positioning and current strategy in further detail. Scott?
Scott Ulm
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Thanks, Jim. December's FOMC meeting resulted in a hawkish pivot, signaling the end of the quantitative easing program and at least four to five federal funds rate hikes in 2022. In addition, the FOMC hinted at a possible reduction of the Fed's balance sheet by midyear 2022. January's FOMC meeting further reinforced the resolve to address the high inflation rate, leaving all options open for an even more aggressive tightening policy on the table, including a possible 50-basis point hike in March. This hawkish shift sent a strong warning to investors to reassess historically tight valuations on most asset categories and for us, particularly US agency MBS. After OAS widened in the Q4 on mortgage-backed securities, there's been a further OAS widening of 15 to 20 basis points in the Q1.
While these levels are now significantly closer to longer-term historical averages, the uncertainty around the policy response to the rising rate of inflation remains high, posing further risk of widening. ARMOUR substantially reduced the risk in our mortgage portfolio early in 2022. We lowered the spread risk in our portfolio by net selling $2.9 billion of MBS, rotating our TBA positions into $600 million specified pool MBS, and $1.6 billion of US Treasuries. This action significantly improved the negative convexity of our portfolio and lowered our implied leverage ratio from 7.5x at the end of Q4 down to 6.5x today. The other side to this wider spread and higher rate environment is better investment opportunities, and ARMOUR is well-positioned to take advantage of them.
Thirty-year agency-backed mortgage rates now exceed 4%, signaling at least a temporary end to the pandemic era refinance wave. This will slow down prepayment p-speeds and potentially increase net margin on the existing portfolio and new investments. Our lower leverage gives us room for two or more terms of leverage to take advantage of improving investment opportunities. We have substantial excess liquidity to support a larger portfolio and hedge book. Because we have 101% of our repo book hedged out with current pay swaps, we have removed much of the uncertainty and added borrowing expense around the exact timing and sizing of the future Fed hikes. If you include our forward-starting swaps, 123% of our repo book is hedged and 90% of our current asset portfolio is hedged.
Our average repo rate today is still historically low at just 13 basis points. ARMOUR is active with 19 different repo counterparties, and approximately 49% of our principal is borrowed with our broker-dealer affiliate, Buckler Securities. We do see potentially significant opportunity around the corner. For today, we maintain a lower risk profile going into the Fed tightening and quantitative easing ending. As we've noted before, we set our dividend policy based on the medium-term outlook in our business. We continue to see our dividend level as appropriate. With that, we'd like to open up for any questions.
Operator
We will now begin the question-and-answer session. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your telephone keypad. If you're using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. If at any time your question has been addressed and you would like to withdraw your question, please press star then two. At this time, we will pause momentarily to assemble our roster. The first question comes from Doug Harter with Credit Suisse. Please go ahead.
Doug Harter
Equity Research Analyst, Credit Suisse
Thanks. Can you talk about the timing of the Q1 portfolio changes that you discussed, and then what conditions you would be looking for in order to kind of move to redeploy that capital or move out of Treasuries back into MBS?
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Sure, Doug. This is Mark. Those portfolio moves were pretty much towards the end of January, and a little bit in February. You know, it's kind of really throughout Q1 so far. To answer your question on reinvestments, you know, look, we're looking for, you know, we think there should be some wider spreads going forward. You know, we'll look at opportunities and when we're comfortable with both the, you know, the yield targets and the risk profile, we'll start to reinvest. We don't. There's no real timing per se where we think we have to invest. We just think there are going to be opportunities coming forward.
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO and President, ARMOUR Residential REIT
The Fed meets 16 March 2022, Doug. I think between now and then they're gonna dribble out through interviews and, you know, conferences with all the Fed members. We're going to learn more and more and more as we get closer to that. We believe when we get there'll be no surprises. In between now and then, we suspect you'll see a little bit more widening. When we start seeing low double-digit returns with all the safety features like good convexity, okay, they're not on the prepayment spectrum. In other words, they're not characteristically could be heavy prepays one month and then, you know, slow the next month, skittish kind of stuff. We get all the good characteristics, you'll see us start investing. You know, we may invest actually before 16 March 2022. We'll see how things develop.
Doug Harter
Equity Research Analyst, Credit Suisse
Got it. Just on the dividend. You know, if you look at the current rate, the $0.10 monthly dividend by your current book value, that would imply, you know, call it a 13% return on book value. You know, do you think that is an achievable return in the current environment or where spreads might go to?
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO and President, ARMOUR Residential REIT
All reinvestment right now is actually marginal money, right? Your overhead is already covered. If you look at the historical leverage in this space, it's a high sevens to high eights kinda range. We're two full turns down from that. If we invest another $2 billion, it's more than achievable. We're just being very careful. You just have, you know, the degradation, you know, recently of the mortgage spreads. As I just said, we're gonna be slow about reinvesting. Yes, it's very achievable.
Scott Ulm
Co-CEO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Not to mention the swap of treasuries into mortgage-backed securities, which doesn't affect the leverage, but certainly, you know, would be where mortgage-backed securities are potentially a much more interesting category. But we kind of like treasuries and their lack of spread risk right now.
Doug Harter
Equity Research Analyst, Credit Suisse
Got it. Thank you.
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO and President, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Thanks.
Operator
The next question comes from Trevor Cranston with JMP Securities. Please go ahead.
Trevor Cranston
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, JMP Securities
Hey, thanks. Good morning. Follow-up on the question about the dividend level. You know, with the moves you guys made so far in Q1, it seems like that would reduce the earnings power of the portfolio, a decent amount, at least over the near term. You guys reiterated that you're comfortable with the dividend level. Can you just sort of share your thinking around, you know, why you guys want to maintain that level, with the yield that the stock is currently trading at versus, you know, maybe taking it down a notch and retaining some more capital for reinvestment in the future? Thanks.
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO and President, ARMOUR Residential REIT
What we've said over the last five, six, seven conference calls is that we look at the dividend rate over the medium term, maybe even a little longer, what is appropriate and what this machine can earn. Although we've been a few cents under it for each of the last few quarters, it's because, you know, despite the fact we lost some book value here, you know, we're being defensive. We just indicated how, you know, two turns of mortgage investment would add $2 billion. I think $1.6 to 1.7 billion of swapping out of Treasuries into mortgages will add a lot of earnings power. We're very comfortable where we are right now with the dividend. We would not expect that to change in the near future.
Trevor Cranston
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, JMP Securities
Okay, got it. On the prepay outlook, it looks like the portfolio had a pretty meaningful drop in speeds in February. Do you guys think that is sort of close to bottomed out, or is there any additional room for that to drop given the spike higher in rates we've seen so far in Q1?
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
You know, our portfolio speeds are pretty low as is. We think there may be a little more room for it to drop a little bit, but we're getting closer to we think the turnover speeds. A little upside to speeds for us on, you know, the amortization earnings forefront, but we think we're close to the bottom here for us in speeds.
Trevor Cranston
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, JMP Securities
Okay. Would that imply that you think the portfolio is pretty fully extended with the durations where they're at currently?
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Yeah, our spec portfolio, yes.
Trevor Cranston
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, JMP Securities
Okay. Appreciate the time. Thank you.
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO and President, ARMOUR Residential REIT
No problem. Very exciting. Hey, just to be clear, Trevor, when he said a little upside, he didn't mean the upside in speed. He meant the upside in potential earnings from reduced amortization expense. Just to be clear there.
Trevor Cranston
Managing Director and Equity Research Analyst, JMP Securities
Yeah, I got that. Thanks.
Operator
Again, if you have a question, please press star then one on a touch tone phone. The next question comes from Christopher Nolan with Ladenburg Thalmann. Please go ahead.
Christopher Nolan
SVP of Equity Research, Ladenburg Thalmann
Hey, guys. Based on your comments, should we be expecting more investments into the 30-year agencies?
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
I would say yes, in that that's where we think there are gonna be opportunities because we expect more spread widening there. You know, there are already some low double-digit opportunities. But like we said, we expect some more spread widening, you know, a little bit rise in rates. Yeah, 30 years is where we'll target.
Christopher Nolan
SVP of Equity Research, Ladenburg Thalmann
Okay. Given your comments, the market's expecting four to five Fed hikes. Given that's been the case for at least a few weeks, should we expect further going into Treasuries coming weeks as you're thinking the market's not fully baking in what's going to transpire. I mean, basically, should we expect further defensive posturing of the portfolio than where it is right now?
Mark Gruber
Chief Investment Officer, ARMOUR Residential REIT
In regard to Scott's comments, that was more of what the Fed was implying in December meeting. What the market's implying now, I think is a little more than that. From a portfolio perspective, I don't think we will get more defensive. You know, we've already moved a lot into Treasuries. We've taken leverage down. You know, I think the next time we talk, we'll probably have hopefully been able to do some reinvesting and added assets as, you know, the opportunities present themselves. I think more defensive is not really where we want to go right now. I think we're set up based on our profile, our risk profile, that we're very comfortable with.
Christopher Nolan
SVP of Equity Research, Ladenburg Thalmann
Great. Are you seeing anything in terms of non-agency investments that you might consider going back into the old CRTs or anything, or is that too premature?
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO and President, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Exactly.
Christopher Nolan
SVP of Equity Research, Ladenburg Thalmann
Yeah. Okay. Thank you, guys.
Jeff Zimmer
Co-CEO and President, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Have a great day. Thanks for calling in.
Operator
This concludes our question-and-answer session. I would like to turn the conference back over to Jim Mountain for any closing remarks.
Jim Mountain
CFO, ARMOUR Residential REIT
Thank you, Andrew, and thank you all for joining us. We look forward to continuing the dialogue in the intervening months. You know where to find us. If questions arise, please feel free to reach out. Until next time, everybody stay safe.
Operator
The conference has now concluded. Thank you for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect.
